title: Structure alone supports efficient visual computation in the Drosophila visual system
authors: Eudald Correig-Fraga, Roger Guimerà, Marta Sales-Pardo
abstract: Understanding the extent to which measured synaptic wiring determines computation remains a central challenge. Here, we couple the proofread adult Drosophila melanogaster connectome to an anatomically faithful model of its eye. Visual information is inputted in the eye model, then passed to the connectome, and finally read from a Kenyon-cell-centered linear decoder. This creates a connectome-only model in which the anatomical graph and eye geometry are fixed and only scalar synaptic gains and neuronal thresholds may be learned. The model supports multitask vision, including color discrimination, shape classification, and numerical discrimination that follows a ratio-dependent scaling characteristic of approximate number perception. To test whether precise connectivity is consequential under wiring economy, we compare the biological graph to randomized ensembles that increasingly preserve biological synaptic constraints. At matched wiring cost, the biological network consistently yields higher accuracy, whereas less constrained rewiring surpasses it at the cost of inflated wiring. These findings indicate that the measured connectivity and eye geometry jointly set efficient operating points for visual computation.
summary: This paper investigates the computational role of fixed anatomical wiring in the fly visual system by creating a connectome-only neural network model. By comparing the actual connectome to randomized versions, the authors show that the specific, measured connectivity is crucial for achieving high computational accuracy under realistic wiring constraints. This suggests that biological structure dictates efficient operating regimes for complex sensory processing.
main_problem: The central challenge is determining how much of the computational efficiency in the visual system is dictated solely by its measured synaptic wiring (connectome).
main_result: The biological connectome achieves higher accuracy than randomized ensembles at matched wiring cost, suggesting that the measured connectivity and eye geometry jointly set efficient operating points for visual computation.
method: The authors built a 'connectome-only' message-passing model, fixing the anatomical graph and eye geometry while only learning synaptic gains and thresholds.
model_or_system: The model uses the full connectome of the *Drosophila* visual system, taking visual input from an anatomically faithful eye model and passing it through the connectome graph to a Kenyon-cell-centered decoder.
key_observables: Task accuracy (color, shape, number discrimination), information propagation dynamics, and computational performance across different connectome ensembles.
important_parameters: Synaptic gains, neuronal thresholds, and the wiring cost (proxied by synaptic distance and count).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that the fixed anatomical wiring and eye geometry are the primary determinants of efficiency, and that performance differences reflect structural constraints rather than optimization differences.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the multi-step computational flow for number discrimination. Figure 2 compares various randomized connectome ensembles (e.g., unconstrained vs. biological) based on wiring constraints and associated statistics. Figure 3 compares task accuracy across these different connectome variants.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by modeling the visual system, details the connectome-only message-passing approach, tests performance on multiple vision tasks, and compares the biological connectome against randomized ensembles to draw conclusions about wiring efficiency.
why_interesting: While focused on biology, the use of graph theory, message passing, and comparing structured vs. random connectivity ensembles mirrors concepts in network science and disordered systems, which can inform models of complex quantum or classical computation.

Computational modeling of numerical discrimination in Drosophila melanogaster. a, Visual stimuli with varying numerosities of colored dots (blue vs. yellow) are processed through an anatomically accurate model of the fly’s compound eye. We reconstruct the 3D positions of retinal neurons from the connectome data, project them onto a 2D plane, and use Voronoi tessellation to map ommatidia, with R7 neuron positions as cell centers. Each ommatidium samples its corresponding region of the visual field, with specific photoreceptors (R1-R8) encoding different color channels based on their biological spectral sensitivities.
